chapters.t: The Shadow of the Lawyer’s Coat
chapters.s: In Deepali’s time, a sharp and gifted young man from the village named Batuknath studied law and began practising in the city. The villagers were proud of him. Batuknath’s story spread beyond the village into the city, and gradually his name became associated not with the speech of the village but with a reputation in the corridors of the courts that Deepali never wished to accept.…

In a glass tower in Hong Kong, the shadow of an unseen power appears for the first time on the horizon of the story. Abhinav warned every young person in the village to be alert to international fraud networks—what proposal was coming from afar, what name was hidden behind it, where the money was going.…

A simple, quiet bank employee from the village, Satyavrat Mehta, begins to waver between duty and conscience. Returning to the city, Satyavrat remembered Budhba’s words and quietly began recording every suspicious transaction in a notebook—the date, the account, where the money moved, how much.…

A young villager named Gop Kumar devotes his life to documents and archives. Hearing this, Gop Kumar continued his collection patiently. He knew he might become a witness, perhaps even the writer, of that final chapter.…

A young man born outside the village, Chandrapal Batra, earns a law degree and becomes entangled in a betting network. Gop Kumar added a new section to his archive—“Distant Relations”—and began preserving names linked with the village but born outside it. Chandrapal became the first entry.…

A gifted young programmer named Raghav is born in the town nearest the village, and the skill in his hands may one day move in either direction—protection or destruction. Gop Kumar entered Raghav’s name in the archive and placed a question mark beside it—an empty space left for the future, to be filled by time.…

A young engineer named Aruni devotes himself to bridges and embankments, giving modern form to the village’s old tradition of flood defence. Taking that lesson to heart, Aruni began attaching a long-term maintenance plan to every project—deciding who would care for each bridge and embankment in the future and who would keep its records.…

A young woman named Devika dedicates her life to carrying the village’s folk-song tradition into the next generation. Devika opened a new school to teach old folk songs to village children—the music branch of the Coconut-Leaf School, where melody was taught alongside letters.…

A sharp young woman named Meera begins raising her voice for the right to digital privacy. Inspired by Budhba’s words, Meera began teaching every village woman and girl the rights of digital safety—how to protect personal information, how to speak against abuse, and where to obtain legal help.…

A young banker named Nishant works for financial inclusion, bringing the village economy into a modern system. Nishant therefore began explaining every financial scheme in simple Maithili—what each account was for, what protection each insurance policy offered, and on what terms each loan worked.…

In this chapter, at last, the child is born whose story far ahead will become the beginning of “Water-Burial Among the Crocodiles”—Nand Aruni. Though the air was still, the pipal leaves rustled softly that night, as if the whole Channa Grove, carrying centuries of memory, were welcoming the new name.…

Counting the years of his own existence, Budhba draws near a startling truth. Gop Kumar marked that calculation specially in his archive and smiled faintly. He did not know how the number—twelve hundred years—would one day be repeated in another language on the tongue of another generation…

A curious young woman named Ananya begins teaching village children to ask questions, carrying Gangesha’s tradition forward. From then on Ananya taught Nand and his classmates to ask a new question every day: Why is this so? Where did this come from? What is the evidence? Nand in particular carried that habit with him for life.…

chapters.t: The First Reckoning of the Splash
chapters.s: At a bridge-construction site, young Nand begins to notice the gap between labouring bodies and the records that are supposed to name them. He starts the diary later called The Reckoning of the Splash, becoming the next witness and carrying Budhba’s old sentence—‘the crocodile eats the body, not the name’—into the modern crisis.
